"The provided text explores the enduring, though outdated, "great man" theory of history. This 19th-century concept posits that exceptional individuals—defined by their talent, courage, and charisma—are the primary drivers of historical change, shaping events through the sheer force of their personality and genius. The article notes that this idea has proven remarkably persistent, surviving challenges from more egalitarian and Marxist social theories, as well as the 1960s academic shift towards "history from below" championed by E.P. Thompson. The Scottish philosopher Thomas Carlyle is identified as a key proponent of this view. For Carlyle, historical figures like Aristotle, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Martin Luther, and the prophet Muhammad were standout heroes who fundamentally altered their world. He believed the role of the general population was simply to passively observe and obediently follow these influential historical actors.

The author dismisses this concept as a "daft idea," yet acknowledges its seductive and long-lived appeal. The text argues that this archetype continues to exist in the modern era, embodied by certain individuals, predominantly men, who genuinely see themselves as heroic. They believe they have a special mission or a sacred duty to act as saviours for their people. These modern figures are characterized by a profound self-assurance, convinced that they "know best" and possess a "unique insight" that others lack. This self-perception is coupled with a ruthlessness and arrogance that allows them to impose their personal views on everyone else. A crucial distinction is made for the contemporary era: unlike Carlyle’s historical heroes, these modern aspirants are typically not heroes at all. Instead, they are seen as anti-heroes or, more precisely, villains. The single defining trait they share with Carlyle's select few is their ability to wield significant power."
[/Thinking]

"The provided text summarizes and critiques the 19th-century "great man" theory of history, which posits that exceptionally talented, charismatic, and courageous individuals single-handedly direct and change historical events through the sheer force of their genius and personality. The article notes that this idea has proven remarkably resilient and "hard to shake," persisting despite the rise of competing academic and social frameworks like egalitarian and Marxist theories, as well as E.P. Thompson's "history from below" school of thought. The Scottish philosopher Thomas Carlyle is presented as a primary advocate for this theory, viewing figures such as Aristotle, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, and the prophet Muhammad as unique heroes who permanently changed the world. In Carlyle's view, the rest of humanity was destined to merely watch, admire, and submissively follow these "makers and shakers."

The author of the article dismisses this concept as a "daft idea" but concedes that it is both seductive and long-lived. The piece then pivots to the modern era, arguing that the archetype of the self-proclaimed great man endures. It describes contemporary figures, mostly men, who believe they are fashioned in a heroic mould, possessing a special mission or sacred duty to lead and save nations. These individuals are defined by a conviction that they "know best," have "unique insight," and are ruthless and arrogant enough to impose their views on all. However, the crucial twist presented is that in the modern context, these figures are not heroes as commonly understood. Instead, they are better classified as anti-heroes or, more pointedly, villains. The one characteristic they share with Carlyle’s historical titans is their capacity to wield significant power."
